preamble: All solutions are thematic, wholly or in part. All clues contain normal definitions but, with 18 of them, the wordplay ignores the thematic element.

solutions.check: grid and clues read from the Guardian's article page and its grid picture, its numbering matching the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: After onset of winter, ordinary leaves disappear (4,3)

indicators.note: the onset of a season is its start, so only the opening letter of winter is used

parts.note: the body part the theme supplies; the wordplay ignores it
ff. is the abbreviation for folios, the leaves of a book

explanation.surface: Once winter sets in, the usual leaves fall away.
explanation.walkthrough: Per the preamble, the wordplay skips this clue's body part; 'leaves' looks like foliage but is the book abbreviation for folios.
explanation.definitionFit: To wear off is a phrasal verb for an effect fading away until it is gone.

parts.note: E is the compass abbreviation for east
the thematic body part, left out of the wordplay
E again for east

explanation.surface: Writing a lament for the poem 'East is East', perhaps as its author has died.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is the opening of Kipling's line 'East is East, and West is West', here read word by word.
explanation.definitionFit: To write an elegy, a mournful poem, is to mourn someone in verse.

clue.text: Arm supporters and order raid on island

indicators.note: to order things is to arrange them, so the letters of raid are rearranged

explanation.surface: A command to supply weapons to backers and send a raid on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arm supporters' reads as a call to weapons; it is the forearm bones.
explanation.definitionFit: These forearm bones run alongside the ulnae and bear the arm's structure, plural of the bone named for the spoke of a wheel.

clue.text: Bones lie over other nameless ones

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece over another comes first

parts.note: a fib is a small lie

indicators.note: nameless means without N, the abbreviation for name

parts.note: the other bones meant here are the ulnae, the forearm bones

explanation.surface: Bones that lie on top of other unnamed bones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'other ones' means other bones, ULNAE, which lose N for name.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the thin outer bones of the lower leg, plural of the Latin for brooch.

clue.text: Nice art stored in suburbs of Leeds, unprotected

parts.note: the thematic body part, left out of the wordplay

indicators.note: something stored in a container sits inside it, so these letters go within the outer pair
suburbs lie on the edge of a city, so only the outer letters of Leeds count

parts.note: Nice is a French city, and in French 'tu es' is 'thou art'

explanation.surface: A piece of artwork from the south of France kept in a Leeds suburb, with no security.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice' looks like an adjective but is the French city, steering to French, where 'tu es' means 'thou art'.
explanation.definitionFit: Without arms (weapons), a person is unarmed and so has nothing to protect themselves with.

clue.text: Send away again for Roman object

parts.note: res is the Latin word for a thing or object
the thematic body part, left out of the wordplay

explanation.surface: Sending back a Roman artefact.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roman' points to Latin, where 'res' means a thing.
explanation.definitionFit: To dispatch a cargo or package a second time is to send it off once more.

indicators.note: food that is cooked is altered, so the letters of meal are rearranged

parts.note: the thematic body part, left out of the wordplay

explanation.surface: A dish of noodles cooked for a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noodle' is pasta in the surface; it is a fool. LAME comes from rearranging MEAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A noodle is a slang word for a fool, a dim-witted person.

clue.text: I'm missing simple directions for waste processors

indicators.note: missing means absent, so the letters of I'm are taken out

parts.note: the contraction is the letters I and M
E, N and S are three compass points

explanation.surface: A complaint that someone hasn't got easy instructions for waste machinery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'simple' loses I and M to give SPLE; then the compass points ENS.
explanation.definitionFit: These organs filter the blood, breaking down worn-out red cells, a waste-handling job.

parts.note: a thematic body part, left out of the wordplay
a game that is over has finished
a thematic body part, left out of the wordplay

explanation.surface: A two-word statement that something is fully done.
explanation.walkthrough: Only OVER comes from the wordplay; HEAD and HEELS are both the theme's parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Being deeply in love, utterly and entirely, is the idiom's meaning.

indicators.note: banks flank a river, so the word for deceived lines both sides of Spain's letter

parts.note: to have someone is to fool them, so had means deceived
E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)

explanation.surface: In Spain, an election was rigged by the banks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banks' looks like financial institutions; it is the verb flanking. 'Poll' is an old word for the head, as in poll tax.
explanation.definitionFit: Poll is an old word for the top of the skull, surviving in poll tax, a tax per person.

clue.text: Middle-class drink kept warm in cups

parts.note: the thematic body part, left out of the wordplay
M is an abbreviation for middle, as in clothing and grade labels
ilk means kind or class, as in 'people of that ilk'

explanation.surface: A suburban family's warm drink, served in cups.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'cups' look like teacups but are bra cups, which keep the breast, and so its milk, warm.
explanation.definitionFit: A mother's natural feed for her baby is held at body temperature within the bra's cups.

clue.text: Origin of limp associated with shank

parts.note: the thematic body part, left out of the wordplay

indicators.note: the origin of something is where it starts, so only the opening letter of limp is taken

explanation.surface: Someone's limp is traced back to a problem with the leg.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives only the L; the shinbone TIBIA comes from the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: The shank is the shin, whose main bone gives the adjective for things relating to it.

clue.text: Nimble player, the German crosses ball oddly

indicators.note: a word that crosses another spans it, so the article's letters straddle what follows

parts.note: der is the masculine form of 'the' in German
the thematic body part, left out of the wordplay

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters of ball are its first and third

explanation.surface: A German footballer, nimble on his feet, makes a strange cross into the box.
explanation.walkthrough: DER spans BL (ball's odd letters); the theme's RIB is slotted in too, ahead of BL.
explanation.definitionFit: A footballer who runs with the ball at his feet past defenders is agile with it.

clue.text: He's on a mission to forget old Freudian desire

parts.note: the thematic body part, left out of the wordplay

indicators.note: forgetting something leaves it out, so the abbreviation for old is dropped

parts.note: an envoy is someone sent on a diplomatic mission

explanation.surface: A diplomat away on duty tries to put aside an old Freudian longing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He's on a mission' reads like a description of a zealot; it simply defines a diplomat.
explanation.definitionFit: Freud's theory said girls feel a jealousy of the male organ, a desire he placed in psychoanalysis.

clue.text: Scrawled articles in Italy about book by egghead

parts.note: il is the Italian masculine 'the', an article
the thematic body part, left out of the wordplay

indicators.note: one piece about another surrounds it, so the article encloses the book's letter

parts.note: il is the Italian masculine 'the', an article
the head of egg is its first letter

explanation.surface: Unreadable writing in Italy about a book by an intellectual.
explanation.walkthrough: Both articles are the Italian masculine 'the'; 'egghead' looks like a boffin but only lends its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing that is scrawled is a careless scribble, often impossible to read.

indicators.note: turned around means facing the other way, so both pieces are read backwards together

parts.note: a scab or rat is a worker who breaks a strike

explanation.surface: A question about whether a scab has formed round the bones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scab' suggests a healing wound; it is the strike-breaker RAT. The question mark marks the definition as plural bones of the ankle.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the bones of the ankle and the back of the foot, seven in each.

clue.text: Crop by taking in some cloth

indicators.note: a word taking something in holds it inside, so the cloth measure goes within by

parts.note: an ell is an old measure for cloth, so it is an amount of cloth

explanation.surface: Trimming a garment by taking in some of its fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crop' and 'taking in' make it a dressmaking scene; the crop here is a bird's food pouch, and an ELL is an old cloth length of about 45 inches.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird's crop is a pouch in its gullet, loosely its stomach, as in a full gut.

clue.text: Record smash hit about a priest's lapidary words

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record

indicators.note: one piece about another surrounds it, so the scrambled letters enclose the rest
smashing something breaks it up, so the letters of hit are scrambled

explanation.surface: A smash-hit record about a priest's last words carved in stone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smash hit' looks like a chart success but splits: 'smash' scrambles HIT to ITH, which goes about A and P. PIT (armpit) is the thematic part, though the wordplay covers it.
explanation.definitionFit: Lapidary means engraved in stone, so words cut on a gravestone are an inscription for the dead.

parts.note: the thematic body part, a slang word for the backside, left out of the wordplay
the thematic body part, left out of the wordplay

explanation.surface: A two-word note calling the British nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: Only BR comes from the wordplay; the theme supplies both body parts. BRASS NECK is British slang for effrontery.
explanation.definitionFit: Nerve in the sense of cheek or audacity is what this British slang phrase names.

parts.note: so means thus, as in 'and so it goes'
the thematic body part, left out of the wordplay

explanation.surface: New dons at a university fast like this.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dons' looks like university teachers; it means puts on clothes. The theme's LIPS sit inside SON, after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: To put on a garment quickly and easily, without fuss, is a phrasal verb for that.

parts.note: the thematic body part, a cell of the body, left out of the wordplay
he lives means he is, existing

explanation.surface: A string player shares a home with a tenor.
explanation.walkthrough: Only IS and T come from the wordplay; CELL is the theme's part.
explanation.definitionFit: One who plays the violoncello, a bowed string instrument held between the knees.

indicators.note: a piece that splits another goes between its letters

indicators.note: short means cut off before its end, so the last letter goes

the thematic body part, an old word for the throat, left out of the wordplay

clue.text: Stones vehicle, black, belonging to relative

parts.note: a car is a vehicle
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
an uncle is a relative

explanation.definitionFit: A carbuncle is a red gemstone, a garnet cut with a rounded top, so gems or precious stones.
